sections.h2: What an evaluation finds in Cambridge homes
sections.html:
Of Cambridge's 41,030 houses (single-detached, semi-detached, row houses and duplexes), 23% were built before 1961 and 60% before 1991, according to the 2021 Census. The typical Cambridge house dates from 1981–1990, and an evaluation is how you find out what that means for yours: the blower door measures air leakage, the advisor inspects the attic, walls, basement, windows and heating system, and the report ranks upgrades by what they'd save.

Cambridge gets about 3,664 heating degree-days a year, a measure of how much heating its climate needs, and its winter design temperature, the cold day heating systems are sized for, is −18.3°C. Those figures come from the climate data for Toronto International, the closest comparable location in that data set (63 km away) in HOT2000, the home-energy software Natural Resources Canada (NRCan) gives energy advisors. That's about 7% less heating demand than the middle of the 70 cities we cover. A moderate heating season with warm summers: fixes should cut heating bills and keep the house cool.

Cambridge summers are hot and humid, so the air sealing and insulation that cut heating bills also keep the house cooler, and a heat pump can do the cooling more efficiently than an old air conditioner.

In the Kitchener-Cambridge-Waterloo area, 71% of households heat mainly with a forced-air furnace; natural gas is the main heating energy for 64% of households and electricity for about 15% (Statistics Canada, 2023). The heating system on the report shapes the recommendations: a forced-air furnace invites a ducted heat pump, electric baseboards a ductless one.

Typical Ontario prices are about $500–$700 for the initial EnerGuide evaluation and $200–$450 for the follow-up, plus HST where it applies. Windfall Ecology Centre charges $500 + HST for the initial evaluation and $250 + HST for the follow-up, Reep Green Solutions charges $540 and $406 with no HST, and City-backed programs in Ottawa and London quote $500–$700 as typical for the first visit. Only assessments from the seven HRSP-approved organizations qualify for the $600 Home Renovation Savings rebate, and none of the seven publishes a price.

Most providers quote the initial (pre-upgrade) and follow-up (post-upgrade) visits separately. Rebate programs that pay on measured improvement need both, so ask for the combined price.

sections.h2: Why the design temperature matters in Cambridge
sections.html:
−18.3°C is the 24th-mildest design temperature of the 70 cities we cover. The F280 calculation works out how much heat each room loses on that design day, from the house's actual walls, windows, air leakage and ceiling insulation.

At −18.3°C, a cold-climate heat pump sized to the calculation can carry most of the season, and the number shows how much backup heat the coldest days need.

In the Kitchener-Cambridge-Waterloo area, 71% of households heat mainly with a forced-air furnace; natural gas is the main heating energy for 64% of households and electricity for about 15% (Statistics Canada, 2023).

Cambridge's hot summers make the cooling side count too. CSA F280 covers cooling capacity as well as heating, so ask for both numbers: a heat pump sized only for winter can be too big for summer, which leaves rooms cool but clammy.

The National Building Code 2020 requires the heating capacity for a house to be worked out with CSA F280, and its list of referenced documents names the 2012 edition, CSA F280-12. Provincial codes can name their own edition and climate values, so ask your designer which ones the calculation uses.

Contractors who size by square footage routinely oversize. An oversized heat pump costs more to buy, cycles on and off, dehumidifies poorly in summer and wears faster. An undersized one leans on backup heat. The F280 report is the evidence either way, and it's worth having before you compare quotes.

About $150–$400 as a standalone calculation (a September 2026 planning range; quotes vary). Many energy advisors bundle it with an EnerGuide evaluation, which also gives the calculation measured air-leakage data instead of an assumption.

radon-testing.title: Radon testing in Cambridge: long-term monitoring, kits and mitigation
radon-testing.description: Radon in Cambridge: Health Canada survey results for the Waterloo Health Unit region (4% above the guideline), how to run a 91-day long-term test, digital monitors versus alpha-track kits, and mitigation by C-NRPP professionals ($2,000–$3,000).
radon-testing.lede: Radon is invisible, has no smell, and is the second-leading cause of lung cancer in Canada. In Health Canada's national survey, 4% of homes tested in the Waterloo Health Unit health region were above the guideline, and only a long-term test tells you about your own house.

glance.sub: the Kitchener-Cambridge, ON (Kitchener-Cambridge-Waterloo CMA) metro area
glance.note: Neighbours' results don't predict yours: test
Health Canada's level for fixing a home

sections.html:
Health Canada's 2012 survey found 4% of 101 homes tested in the Waterloo Health Unit health region above the guideline. The larger 2024 Cross-Canada survey reports 10.2% (1 in 10) of houses at or above the guideline for the Kitchener-Cambridge, ON (Kitchener-Cambridge-Waterloo CMA) metro area.

The two surveys aren't directly comparable: the 2024 study pooled about 69,000 volunteer tests and more of them were taken in basements, which partly explains its higher numbers. Neither can tell you about a single house, because neighbouring homes can differ widely.

sections.h2: Long-term monitoring: how to test properly
sections.html:
Health Canada's measurement guide asks for a long-term test with at least 91 days in the heating season, when closed windows and the stack effect make readings higher, so the result is a conservative estimate of the yearly average. It recommends testing for 3 to 12 months. Our radon testing guide walks through each step.

Place the detector on the lowest level where someone spends more than four hours a day, at least 30 cm above the floor and 30 cm from walls, and at least 1 m from vents, windows and doors; avoid kitchens, laundry rooms and bathrooms. The choice of device:

  • Alpha track detectors record radon's alpha particles on a plastic film; you mail them to a lab when the test ends. A long-term kit costs about $30–$80 including the lab fee (Windsor-Essex County Health Unit).
  • Electret ion chambers lose charge as radon ionizes the air inside; a lab reads the voltage drop.
  • Digital (electronic) monitors read continuously and show results on a screen or an app, and cost more (Lung Saskatchewan sells one for $189). For a long-term test, Health Canada says to use one that has passed C-NRPP performance testing, and it still has to run at least three months.
  • Continuous monitoring after mitigation: a digital monitor left running lets you watch for changes between the follow-up long-term tests Health Canada recommends.

• There's no provincial free-kit program, but many Ontario public libraries lend digital radon monitors free with a library card, among them Hamilton, Vaughan, Guelph, Kingston Frontenac, Greater Sudbury, Thunder Bay, Brantford and Waterloo.
  • For a professional measurement or mitigation, search the C-NRPP directory by your Cambridge postal code; it lists certified measurement and mitigation professionals.

sections.h2: If your level is high: mitigation
sections.html:
Health Canada recommends fixing levels above 200 Bq/m³ within a year, and sooner the higher the level. The usual fix is a sub-slab depressurization system (a sealed pipe through the floor and a fan venting outside), which Health Canada says costs about $2,000 to $3,000 including material and labour and cuts radon by more than 80% in most homes. Hire a professional certified for mitigation under C-NRPP. After a system goes in:

  • A C-NRPP professional runs a short test starting at least 24 hours after the fan is turned on.
  • A long-term three-month test follows in the next fall or winter, done by a company other than the installer.
  • With an active system, Health Canada recommends a long-term test within two years of activation and every five years after that, and again after renovations.
  • Check the system's pressure gauge (manometer) regularly and never switch the fan off. It costs about $50 to $75 a year to run; a replacement fan is $200 to $300.

• Since January 1, 2025, the Ontario Building Code requires new houses to include a soil-gas barrier and a radon rough-in.
  • Tarion's new-home warranty covers radon remediation for seven years from possession, and the Canadian Lung Association's Lungs Matter program offers up to $1,500 toward mitigation for households with low to moderate incomes or a lung cancer diagnosis.

faq.a: Health Canada's 2012 survey found 4% of 101 homes tested in the Waterloo Health Unit health region above the guideline. The larger 2024 Cross-Canada survey reports 10.2% (1 in 10) of houses at or above the guideline for the Kitchener-Cambridge, ON (Kitchener-Cambridge-Waterloo CMA) metro area. Any home can have high radon, so Health Canada recommends testing every home.

faq.q: How long should a radon test take?
faq.a: At least 91 days, in the heating season. Health Canada recommends 3 to 12 months; short tests can't tell you your long-term average.

faq.q: Where can I get a radon test kit in Cambridge?
faq.a: There's no provincial free-kit program, but many Ontario public libraries lend digital radon monitors free with a library card, among them Hamilton, Vaughan, Guelph, Kingston Frontenac, Greater Sudbury, Thunder Bay, Brantford and Waterloo. Hardware stores and lung associations also sell long-term kits, for about $30–$80 including the lab fee.

faq.q: Digital radon monitor or alpha-track kit?
faq.a: An alpha-track kit is the cheaper long-term test: it sits for three months or more and goes to a lab. A digital monitor shows readings as it goes and can keep running after mitigation; for a long-term result, use one that has passed C-NRPP testing and run it for at least three months.

faq.q: What does radon mitigation cost?
faq.a: Health Canada puts a sub-slab depressurization system at about $2,000 to $3,000 including material and labour, plus about $50 to $75 a year to run the fan. Hire a C-NRPP-certified mitigation professional.

faq.q: Should I keep monitoring after mitigation?
faq.a: Yes. Health Canada recommends a long-term test in the following heating season, another within two years of activation, and one every five years after that. A digital monitor running in between shows if anything changes.

Single-detached houses make up 57% of Cambridge's households; many have an attached garage, another reason to put an alarm near the door into the house.

• Alarms next to sleeping areas and on every storey, tested monthly and replaced by their end-of-life date (usually 7 to 10 years).

mold-testing.h1: Mould and indoor air quality testing in Cambridge
mold-testing.title: Mould and indoor air quality (IAQ) testing in Cambridge: air sampling, inspection and remediation
mold-testing.description: Mould inspection and indoor air quality testing in Cambridge: when mold sampling is worth it, why cold winters cause condensation, the CMHC and Health Canada size rules for cleanup, and when to hire a remediation contractor.
mold-testing.lede: Mould sampling tells you whether there's a hidden mould problem and roughly where. It doesn't tell you why, and fixing the moisture source is the actual cure. Here's how to inspect a home in Cambridge, when air quality testing helps, and how much cleanup you can safely do yourself.

glance.note: Older basements and walls have more damp spots

glance.sub: or if it keeps coming back

glance.note: Ask which accredited lab reads the samples

sections.h2: Why mould shows up in Cambridge homes
sections.html:
Cambridge gets about 3,664 heating degree-days a year, a measure of how much heating its climate needs, and its winter design temperature, the cold day heating systems are sized for, is −18.3°C. Those figures come from the climate data for Toronto International, the closest comparable location in that data set (63 km away) in HOT2000, the home-energy software Natural Resources Canada (NRCan) gives energy advisors. On cold days, exterior corners, closets on outside walls and window frames get cold enough for condensation, which is where mould usually starts in Cambridge houses.

Summer is the second mould season in Cambridge: warm, humid outdoor air condenses on cool basement walls and floors. A dehumidifier that keeps the basement in Health Canada's 30–50% humidity range is the usual fix.

Of Cambridge's 41,030 houses (single-detached, semi-detached, row houses and duplexes), 23% were built before 1961 and 60% before 1991, according to the 2021 Census. Older basements without a moisture barrier and houses that were air-sealed without adding ventilation are common trouble spots.

sections.h2: Mould inspection: when sampling is worth it
sections.html:
Start by looking and smelling: stains, discoloured patches, peeling paint and a musty odour, especially in basements, bathrooms, window frames and closets on outside walls. Health Canada says measuring mould concentrations or identifying species is usually unnecessary.

No Canadian province has a mandatory mould standard for homes. Health Canada's guideline sets no numerical limit: it says to fix moisture problems and clean up visible mould.

Air or surface sampling helps in three cases:

  • You smell mustiness but can't find the source.
  • After a leak or flood, to check that cleanup worked.
  • Before buying an older house with signs of past water damage.

sections.h2: Cleanup and remediation: the size rules
sections.html:
CMHC and Health Canada sort mould by size, and the size decides who should clean it up:

SizeWhat countsWho should clean it
SmallOne to three patches, each smaller than 1 m²A healthy homeowner, with water and unscented dish detergent (CMHC)
MediumMore than three patches, or patches between 1 and 3 m² (32 square feet)Trained help; homeowners only with training and precautions
LargeA patch larger than 3 m², or many patches through the houseA qualified mould remediation contractor (CMHC)
  • Fix the moisture source first: a leak, poor drainage, or condensation from high humidity. Health Canada recommends 30–50% relative humidity.
  • For a small cleanup, wear safety glasses or goggles, an N95 mask if possible and household rubber gloves. People at risk from mould shouldn't clean it and should stay away.
  • Health Canada suggests professional help for extensive mould, especially growth that keeps coming back after cleaning.

sections.h2: Choosing a tester, lab or remediation contractor
sections.html:
Ask any Cambridge tester which lab analyzes their samples, and look for one accredited under AIHA's EMLAP program for environmental microbiology. Pair sampling with a ventilation and humidity assessment, which finds the cause. For remediation, get two or three written quotes that describe containment, what will be removed and how the area is cleaned.

Ventilation and humidity assessments in Cambridge · Our mould and indoor air quality guide

faq.q: How much does mould testing cost in Cambridge?
faq.a: We found no reputable Canadian source for the cost of a professional mould assessment, so get two or three written quotes and ask how many samples are included, which lab analyzes them and what the report covers.

faq.q: Do I need a test if I can see mould?
faq.a: Usually not. Visible mould needs cleanup and a fix for the moisture source. Testing helps most when you suspect mould you can't see.

faq.q: How much mould can I clean myself?
faq.a: CMHC says a healthy homeowner can clean one to three patches, each under 1 m², with water and unscented dish detergent. Larger areas need trained help or a remediation contractor.

faq.q: When should I hire a mould remediation contractor?
faq.a: For a single patch over 3 m², many patches through the house, or mould that keeps coming back after cleaning (CMHC, Health Canada).

faq.q: Is there a legal mould limit for homes in Canada?
faq.a: No. Health Canada sets no numerical limit; its guidance is to control moisture and clean up mould. Quebec has a voluntary handling standard.

asbestos-testing.lede: About 24,600 Cambridge houses (60%) were built before 1991, when asbestos still turned up in insulation, flooring, plaster and duct wrap. A lab test before renovation is the only way to know.

sections.h2: Where asbestos shows up in Cambridge houses
sections.html:
Of Cambridge's 41,030 houses (single-detached, semi-detached, row houses and duplexes), 23% were built before 1961 and 60% before 1991, according to the 2021 Census.

  • Vermiculite attic insulation: loose, pebbly, grey-brown or silver-gold granules.
  • Vinyl floor tiles and their adhesive, textured ceilings and some plaster.

In Ontario, O. Reg. 278/05 sets the rules for contractors working with asbestos. Owners must have materials checked before arranging renovation or demolition work, but that duty doesn't apply to an owner-occupied house or a building of four units or fewer, so testing your own home is your decision.

Whatever the rules, don't sand, cut or remove suspect material yourself before it's tested.

A trained assessor takes small samples, and an accredited lab analyzes them; plan on about $50–$150 per sample. Asbestos labs in Canada are typically accredited under NIST's NVLAP program.

sections.h2: If it's positive: abatement and removal
sections.html:
Leave the material alone until a plan is in place. For vermiculite, Health Canada says not to use the attic for storage, to keep children out and to seal gaps around the attic hatch, light fixtures and outlets, and to hire professionals trained to handle asbestos if you plan to renovate.

In Ontario: Ontario's O. Reg. 278/05 classes contractor work as Type 1, 2 or 3, each with its own procedures and training, and requires advance notice for Type 3 and some Type 2 jobs. The province's waste rules apply to anyone: asbestos waste can leave the site only for a disposal site whose operator has agreed to accept it, in rigid, sealed, impermeable containers that are marked.

Abatement is quoted separately from testing. Get two or three written quotes that describe containment, what will be removed and how the waste will be disposed of.

faq.a: Leave it alone, keep the attic closed, and have it sampled before any attic work. Health Canada advises against disturbing it or removing it yourself.

lead-paint-testing.title: Lead paint testing in Cambridge: at-risk homes, testing and safe abatement
lead-paint-testing.description: 23% of Cambridge's houses were built before 1961, when lead paint was common. How to test with $15–$40 swabs or a lab, and how to renovate safely.
lead-paint-testing.lede: Health Canada says a home built before 1960 probably has lead paint somewhere. That's 23% of Cambridge's houses (built before 1961, per the 2021 Census), plus exterior paint on many of the 37% built from 1961 to 1990.

glance.note: Probably has lead paint somewhere (Health Canada)
Exterior paint may contain lead
A quick screen, not proof

sections.h2: Which Cambridge homes are at risk
sections.html:
Of Cambridge's 41,030 houses (single-detached, semi-detached, row houses and duplexes), 23% were built before 1961 and 60% before 1991, according to the 2021 Census.

  • Built before 1960: probably has lead-based paint (Health Canada).
  • Built 1960–1990: exterior paint may contain lead, and interior paint may contain smaller amounts.
  • Built after 1990: consumer paints were virtually lead-free by then.

• Swab kits ($15–$40) give a quick screen of the surfaces you plan to disturb.
  • For certainty, send paint chips to a lab accredited under AIHA's ELLAP program, or hire a firm with an X-ray fluorescence (XRF) analyzer.
  • Test before sanding, stripping or replacing old windows and trim.

Our lead paint guide.

sections.h2: If it's positive: lead paint abatement
sections.html:
Health Canada says leaving lead-based paint alone is sometimes safer than removing it, as long as it isn't chipping or within children's reach, and covering it with wallpaper, wallboard or panelling adds protection. Paint that's chipping, flaking or within reach of children is a serious hazard and has to come off carefully; consider hiring an expert before you start.

No province has a lead-paint rule aimed at homeowners, but contractors in B.C. must include lead in pre-renovation and demolition hazard inspections, and in Yukon before demolition. If you do the work yourself, Health Canada's precautions are:

  • Don't use sanders, heat guns or blowlamps: they create toxic dust and fumes. For do-it-yourself work, Health Canada suggests a chemical paint-stripper paste applied with a brush.
  • Move furniture out or cover it with plastic, seal doorways and vents with plastic sheeting and tape, and run a fan blowing out through an open window.
  • Wear goggles, gloves and a good-quality mask, work in 10-minute stretches with breaks outdoors, and don't eat, drink or smoke in the work area.
  • Clean up daily: put scrapings in a sealed container marked Hazardous Waste, follow your municipality's disposal instructions, and wipe surfaces with a damp cloth you throw away.
  • Keep children and pregnant people away until the work is done; Health Canada says there is no known safe level of lead exposure.

faq.q: Does my Cambridge house have lead paint?
faq.a: If it was built before 1960, probably; 1960–1990, possibly on the exterior. Test the surfaces you plan to disturb.

faq.q: Are lead test swabs reliable?
faq.a: They are a useful screen. For renovation decisions, confirm with a lab analysis of paint chips or an XRF reading.

faq.q: What does lead paint testing cost?
faq.a: Swab kits run about $15–$40; lab analysis and XRF testing cost more and are quoted by the firm.

faq.q: Should I remove lead paint or cover it?
faq.a: Health Canada says leaving it alone or covering it with wallpaper, wallboard or panelling is sometimes safer than removing it, as long as it isn't chipping or within children's reach. Never sand it or use a heat gun, and consider hiring an expert for removal.

commercial-energy-audit.description: Commercial and multi-unit building energy audits in Cambridge: ASHRAE levels, 2 reporting rules that apply, and 5 utility or government incentives for audits and studies.
commercial-energy-audit.lede: Offices, apartment buildings, retail and industrial sites get engineering energy audits rather than EnerGuide evaluations. Here's what applies in Cambridge: 2 mandatory reporting rules and 5 incentive programs we found for audits and studies.

sections.h2: Reporting rules that apply in Cambridge
sections.html:
• No city-specific rule found (none found): No municipal energy/water benchmarking, reporting or building-performance by-law found; provincial rules apply (see rules.provinces.ON).
  • Energy and Water Reporting and Benchmarking (EWRB) - O. Reg. 506/18 (in force): Buildings 50,000 sq ft (4,645 m2) and larger. Buildings 100,000 sq ft and larger need a certified professional to verify data in the first reporting year and every five years after. Source
  • Broader Public Sector energy reporting - O. Reg. 25/23 (in force): Applies by organization type (public agencies), not floor area. Source

• Commercial Custom Audits & Studies - Energy Assessments and Meters (Enbridge Gas (Ontario)): Pays up to 50% of eligible costs for energy audits, engineering feasibility studies, steam trap surveys/audits, air and water balancing and metering. The cap depends on the address's previous-year gas use: up to $6,000 (100,000 to under 3,000,000 m3), up to $10,000 (3,000,000 to under 10,000,000 m3), up to $20,000 (10,000,000 m3+, institutions only). Institutions max $20,000 per project; other commercial sectors max $10,000 per project. Details
  • Affordable Housing Multi-Residential Program - energy assessment (Enbridge Gas (Ontario)): Up to $8,000 for an energy assessment (up to $40,000 per housing provider) to find natural gas savings in affordable housing buildings. Details
  • Save on Energy Small Business Program (Save on Energy (IESO)): Free on-site assessment by qualified Save on Energy representatives, then free installed upgrades: up to $3,000 for lighting and up to $2,500 for refrigeration and smart thermostats (up to $5,500 total). Details
  • Existing Building Commissioning (EBCx) Program (Save on Energy (IESO)): Funds retro-commissioning. Investigation phase: up to $0.06 per sq ft, max $50,000 per application or 75% of the participant's cost for the commissioning provider. Implementation and persistence phases: $0.03 per kWh of confirmed/persisting savings (each capped at 30% of annual consumption or $50,000, whichever is lower). Details
  • XLerate Program - Project Feasibility Study funding (Save on Energy (IESO)): Project feasibility study (PFS) funding at a 50% cost share; project incentives of $300/MWh up to 75% of eligible costs (max $15 million per project). Details

• Level 1, walk-through: a site visit and bill review that benchmarks the building and lists low-cost measures.
  • Level 2, energy survey and analysis: where the energy goes, with savings and cost estimates per measure. Most incentive applications use this level.
  • Level 3, detailed analysis: monitoring and modelling for capital-intensive projects.

Ask which level a quote covers. Audits are done by engineering firms and energy consultants; look for a P.Eng. and credentials such as the Certified Energy Manager (CEM). How commercial energy audits work.

Check eligibility and pre-approval rules before you commission the audit.
